analysis.one_liner: Bans unfair practices by meat, poultry, and crop buyers and lets farmers sue, with a new USDA enforcement office.
analysis.headline: The Competitive and Fair Agricultural Markets Act of 2007 never got a committee vote or floor vote; it died in the Senate Agriculture Committee at the end of the 110th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Sponsored by Sen. Tom Harkin with bipartisan cosponsorship (8 cosponsors: 6 D, 2 R, including Sens. Enzi and Thomas), the bill would have created an Office of Special Counsel for Competition Matters within USDA to investigate and prosecute violations of the Packers and Stockyards Act and the new unfair-practice prohibitions. It would have banned unfair, discriminatory, or deceptive practices by meatpackers, poultry dealers, processors, and crop buyers; given poultry growers the same legal protections as other livestock producers; stripped out the requirement to prove 'competitive injury'; voided contract confidentiality clauses; restricted mandatory arbitration; gave contract producers a 3-day cancellation right, 180-day termination notice plus cure rights for large capital investments, and a ban on forced additional capital investments; voided out-of-state choice-of-law and venue provisions; and raised the civil penalty ceiling for live poultry dealer violations from $10,000 to $22,000. It was introduced on 2007-02-15 and referred to the Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee, where no further action was taken before Congress ended on 2009-01-03.
analysis.who_benefits: Family farmers and ranchers — including poultry growers, contract livestock producers, and crop producers — who would have gained a dedicated prosecutor for unfair buyer practices, new contract protections (disclosure, cancellation, termination-notice and cure rights, limits on forced capital investment), the right to sue for damages with attorneys' fees, and the ability to join bargaining associations without retaliation.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes an Office of Special Counsel for Competition Matters within USDA to investigate and prosecute violations of the new prohibitions and the Packers and Stockyards Act, with Senate-confirmed leadership and authority to bring civil or administrative actions directly.

Makes any unfair, unjustly discriminatory, or deceptive act or anti-competitive practice unlawful regardless of whether it can be shown to have harmed competition and regardless of any claimed business justification, eliminating the 'competitive injury' defense that had made enforcement difficult.

Extends Packers and Stockyards Act protections to live poultry dealers and poultry growers by removing the 'slaughter' requirement from the definitions, and authorizes temporary injunctions for poultry-care cases.

Voiding contract confidentiality clauses and requiring cover-page disclosure of key terms (duration, termination, payment factors, environmental responsibility, etc.); a 3-business-day right to cancel production contracts; for contracts requiring $100,000+ capital investment, 180 days' written notice of termination with a right to cure and a ban on forcing additional capital investments beyond the initial requirement.
Prohibits interference with producers' right to join associations of producers, prohibits retaliation for membership, and requires covered persons to bargain in good faith with such associations.

Restricting mandatory arbitration (arbitration only if both parties agree after a dispute arises) and voiding out-of-state choice-of-law and venue provisions that forced farmers to litigate far from home.
Raising the maximum civil penalty for live poultry dealer violations from $10,000 to $22,000.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpackers, poultry integrators, processors, handlers, dealers, and large commodity buyers would have borne compliance costs, litigation risk, and the possibility of damages awards, injunctions, and penalties. Some would have had to renegotiate contract terms or abandoned practices like mandatory confidentiality, mandatory arbitration, and unilateral termination without notice.

drawbacks.text: Eliminating the 'competitive injury' requirement means virtually any unfavorable contract term or preference could be challenged as unfair even without proof of market harm, raising the risk of litigation over ordinary commercial arrangements.

The prohibition on requiring additional capital investments beyond the initial contract (with exceptions) could complicate legitimate facility upgrades and restructuring that integrators argue are needed for food safety, animal welfare, or efficiency.
Costs imposed on packers and integrators could be partially passed through to consumers or to growers in other contract terms over time, an honest cost that supporters would have to acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For family farmers and ranchers, especially poultry growers and contract livestock producers who face concentrated buyer markets, the bill's contract protections, dedicated enforcement office, and removal of the competitive-injury requirement would have been substantial and low-cost to them directly, with enforcement costs borne by taxpayers and litigation costs shifted toward covered persons. For processors and integrators, compliance and litigation exposure would be significant, and some costs might ultimately flow to consumers. On balance the benefits to a numerically large and economically vulnerable group of producers outweigh the compliance burdens on large agricultural buyers, though the breadth of the 'no competitive injury required' standard would have invited disputes over ordinary commercial practices.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee on February 15, 2007, and no committee vote, markup, or floor action ever followed before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Harkin (D-IA) introduced S. 622 on February 15, 2007, for himself and six other senators.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry on the day of introduction.
No further action — no committee markup, vote, or floor consideration — was taken on the bill for the remainder of the 110th Congress.

The bill attracted 8 cosponsors (6 Democrats and 2 Republicans, including Sens. Michael Enzi and Craig Thomas), showing initial bipartisan interest, but the bill died in committee without a recorded vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpackers, poultry integrators, and processors gained by avoiding the contract restrictions, disclosure requirements, arbitration limits, and litigation exposure the bill would have imposed; no competing measure overrode these interests, so the status quo under the Packers and Stockyards Act remained unchanged during the 110th Congress.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 15, 2007, and delivered introductory remarks in the Senate.

for.name: 8 cosponsors (6 D, 2 R)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Michael Enzi (R-WY) and Craig Thomas (R-WY).

for.name: Contract farmers and poultry growers
for.what_they_did: The bill was designed to protect contract livestock and poultry producers from unfair buyer practices; no organization lobbying in favor is documented in the provided record.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee leadership (110th Congress)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on S. 622 during the 110th Congress, allowing it to die at the end of the session without floor consideration.

against.name: Meatpacking, poultry, and agricultural processing industries
against.what_they_did: Would have been subject to the bill's new prohibitions, contract restrictions, and litigation exposure; opposition activity is not documented in the provided record but is consistent with the industry's general resistance to expanded Packers and Stockyards Act enforcement.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship (1 Democratic sponsor, 6 Democratic and 2 Republican cosponsors), but it never reached a recorded vote, so party-line patterns cannot be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would have expanded Packers and Stockyards Act enforcement against packers and live poultry dealers, removed the competitive-injury requirement, and raised penalties, directly increasing litigation and compliance costs for large processing firms that buy from contract growers.

industries.industry: Agricultural contracting and integration (e.g., contract poultry and hog production systems)
industries.note: Integrators would have faced mandatory contract disclosures, cancellation and termination-notice rights for growers, limits on forced capital investment, voided confidentiality and out-of-state venue clauses, and restrictions on mandatory arbitration — all of which constrain their control over contract terms.

industries.industry: Crop and commodity handlers, dealers, and processors
industries.note: New prohibitions on unfair, discriminatory, or deceptive practices and on price manipulation in crop markets would have applied to handlers, dealers, processors, and commission merchants, exposing them to civil suits and injunctions.
